## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Two–stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental-variables (IV) regression.  

Justification  
• The outcome (log GDP pc 1995) and suspected causal regressor (institutional quality 1985-95) are measured once per country ⇒ panel and time-series methods such as DiD/event study are inapplicable.  
• Institutions are endogenous (reverse causality and omitted geography/culture).  
• We have a historically predetermined, plausibly exogenous instrument—log settler mortality—which varies sharply across the same cross-section.  
Hence a cross-sectional IV design is the natural, rigorous choice.

## 2. Treatment and Control  
Because treatment is continuous, “treated” ≈ countries with better institutions.  

• Treatment variable: INSTᵢ = average 1985-95 protection from expropriation risk (0–10, higher = better).  
• Instrument: Zᵢ = log( settler mortality rate ) in colony i (higher = worse disease environment).  
  – No discrete cut-off; every country’s Zᵢ serves as quasi-random variation in treatment intensity.  
• Control group: Countries with high settler mortality (therefore predicted low INST) provide the counterfactual for low-mortality colonies.  
• Timing: Zᵢ measured 17th–19th c. → INSTᵢ 1985-95 → GDPᵢ 1995.  

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions (IV)  
A1. Relevance: Cov(Zᵢ , INSTᵢ) ≠ 0.  
 Plausibility: Historical evidence that Europeans created inclusive institutions where they could settle; empirical first stage expected strong (F-stat > 10).  

A2. Exclusion: Conditional on controls, settler mortality affects 1995 GDP only through its impact on current institutions.  
 Plausibility: Reasonable—malaria‐based mortality circa 1700 should not directly depress 1995 GDP once modern-era disease environment, geography, trade access, etc. are controlled for. Still controversial; see Threats.  

A3. Independence (as-good-as-random): Zᵢ is not correlated with unobservable determinants of GDP after controls (e.g., culture, soil quality).  
 Plausibility: More credible than OLS, but some geographic correlates remain; addressed with rich controls and sensitivity checks.  

A4. Monotonicity / no defiers: A lower mortality environment never produces systematically worse institutions, i.e., settlers do not purposely adopt extractive institutions where they can thrive.  
 Plausibility: Historical narrative supports.  

A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): One country’s historical mortality does not affect another’s institutions/GDP except through its own. Plausible in cross-section.

## 4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  

T1. Direct effect of historical disease environment on modern GDP (violates exclusion).  
  • Add controls for modern malaria ecology, absolute latitude, distance to tropics/coast, continent dummies.  
  • Show IV results are robust to including contemporary health proxies (e.g., 1960 malaria prevalence).  
  • Perform placebo test: regress 1995 life expectancy on instrument; if strong, caution.  

T2. Measurement error in settler mortality or institutions.  
  • Use multiple historical sources; instrument with both Bishop & Soldier mortality → over-ID test (Hansen J).  
  • Show robustness to excluding outliers with imprecise figures (e.g., very small sample size colonies).  

T3. Sample selection / survivorship: Only colonies that became independent states enter the sample.  
  • Document sample coverage; check whether excluded territories differ systematically.  
  • Re-estimate dropping very small islands or high-income offshore financial centers.  

## 5. R Code Outline  

```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast 2SLS
library(modelsummary)

# ---- 1. Load Data ----
df <- read_csv("colonies_settlerMortality.csv")   # one row per country

# expected columns:
# country, log_gdp95, inst_8595, log_settler_mort, latitude,
# africa, asia, americas, distance_coast, brit_legal, fr_legal

# ---- 2. Variable Construction ----
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(
    log_gdp95    = log_gdp95,                   # already logged
    institutions = inst_8595 / 10,              # rescale 0–1
    log_mort     = log_settler_mort,            # instrument
    abs_lat      = abs(latitude),
    brit         = as.integer(brit_legal==1),
    french       = as.integer(fr_legal==1)
  )

# ---- 3. Main Specification ----
# 2SLS: log GDP on institutions, IV = settler mortality, with controls
iv_formula <- log_gdp95 ~ institutions + abs_lat + distance_coast +
              africa + asia + americas + brit + french | 
              log_mort + abs_lat + distance_coast +
              africa + asia + americas + brit + french

iv_main <- feols(iv_formula, data = df, se = "hetero")

# First-stage F-stat
screenreg <- modelsummary(list(iv_main),
                          statistic = "statistic", 
                          glance_custom = list(
                            first_stage_F = ~wald_f(iv_main)
                          ))

# ---- 4. Robustness Check: add malaria prevalence 1960 ----
iv_formula_rb <- update(iv_formula, . ~ . + malaria1960 | . )
iv_rb <- feols(iv_formula_rb, data = df, se = "hetero")

modelsummary(list("Main IV" = iv_main,
                  "Add Malaria Control" = iv_rb),
             stars = TRUE, output = "markdown")
```

## 6. Expected Results  
Prior: Better institutions raise income.  
Magnitude guess: A 1-standard-deviation improvement in institutions (≈ 1.5 points on 0–10 scale) increases log GDP per capita by roughly 0.7 – 1.0 (i.e., 100–170 percent higher income). Direction: positive.

## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)  

C1: Strong first-stage (F > 10)  … 1  
C2: Exclusion plausible / no direct path … 0.5  
C3: Independence from unobservables given controls … 0.5  
C4: No defiers / monotonicity … 1  
C5: SUTVA … 1  

Total ≈ 4/5.
